title: Giving your opinion
why: The first lesson of level B1: you learn to give your opinion, say whether you agree and weigh the pros and cons. You reuse the comparative and the hif'il from unit 10 in small everyday debates (vacations, city or countryside, working from home).

{"lessons": ["

In my opinion…

To give your opinion, three phrases come up all the time:

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
לְדַעְתִּיleda'atiin my opinion (word for word: \"according to my opinion\")
אֲנִי חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁ… / אֲנִי חוֹשֶׁבֶת שֶׁ…ani khoshev she… / ani khoshevet she…I think that… (man / woman)
נִרְאֶה לִי שֶׁ…nir'e li she…it seems to me that…

\"That\" is שֶׁ (she). In English you can often leave \"that\" out (\"I think it's good\"), but in Hebrew it's required. Like בְּ or וְ, it attaches to the next word, which often gets a dot (dagesh):

אֲנִי חוֹשֶׁבֶת שֶׁזֶּה רַעְיוֹן טוֹב.I think that it's a good idea. [ani khoshevet she-ze ra'ayon tov]
נִרְאֶה לִי שֶׁהַכְּפָר יוֹתֵר שָׁקֵט.It seems to me that the village is quieter. [nir'e li she-ha-kfar yoter shaket]

חוֹשֵׁב agrees like any present-tense verb: a man says חוֹשֵׁב, a woman חוֹשֶׁבֶת. On the other hand, לְדַעְתִּי and נִרְאֶה לִי never change: very handy when you're talking fast!

", "

Agreeing, disagreeing

מַסְכִּים is a hif'il verb, like מַתְחִיל or מַרְגִּישׁ (unit 10). Just like English \"I agree,\" Hebrew uses a simple present-tense verb, with no \"to be.\" Like any present-tense verb, it agrees in gender and number:

HebrewPronunciationWho's speaking
אֲנִי מַסְכִּיםani maskima man
אֲנִי מַסְכִּימָהani maskimaa woman
אֲנַחְנוּ מַסְכִּימִיםanakhnu maskimima group (mixed or all men)
אֲנַחְנוּ מַסְכִּימוֹתanakhnu maskimota group of women

\"With you\": אִתְּךָ (itkha) to a man, אִתָּךְ (itakh) to a woman.

אֲנִי לֹא מַסְכִּימָה אִתְּךָ.I don't agree with you. (a woman to a man) [ani lo maskima itkha]

To soften things: לֹא כָּל כָּךְ (not really), זֶה תָּלוּי (it depends), נָכוֹן (that's true), בְּדִיּוּק (exactly). To ask someone's opinion: מָה דַּעְתְּךָ? (ma da'atkha, to a man), מָה דַּעְתֵּךְ? (ma da'atekh, to a woman).

The trap: \"what do you think of…?\" isn't said with מִ (\"from\"). In Hebrew you think \"on\" something, a bit like \"about\": מָה דַּעְתֵּךְ עַל הַכְּפָר? (what do you think of the countryside?)

", "

Weighing the pros and cons

To present two sides of a question: מִצַּד אֶחָד… מִצַּד שֵׁנִי… (mi-tsad ekhad… mi-tsad sheni…), exactly like \"on the one hand… on the other hand…\".

מִצַּד אֶחָד, בָּעִיר יֵשׁ הַכֹּל. מִצַּד שֵׁנִי, יֵשׁ הַרְבֵּה רַעַשׁ.On the one hand, the city has everything. On the other hand, there's a lot of noise. [mi-tsad ekhad, ba-ir yesh ha-kol. mi-tsad sheni, yesh harbe ra'ash]

Debate words: יִתְרוֹן (yitron, advantage) and חִסָּרוֹן (khisaron, disadvantage). And the comparative from unit 10 comes in handy all the time: יוֹתֵר שָׁקֵט (quieter), פָּחוֹת רוֹעֵשׁ (less noisy).

לְדַעְתִּי, בַּכְּפָר יֵשׁ יִתְרוֹן גָּדוֹל: הַשֶּׁקֶט.In my opinion, the countryside has one big advantage: the peace and quiet. [leda'ati, ba-kfar yesh yitron gadol: ha-sheket]

In Israel, people discuss things frankly and with energy: אֲנִי לֹא מַסְכִּים isn't rude at all. To soften it, add אוּלַי (maybe) or start with נִרְאֶה לִי.
